title: Cross-Site Scripting XSS: Detection and Prevention
summary: Identifying reflected, stored and DOM-based XSS and preventing recurrence.
content:
# Cross-Site Scripting (XSS): Detection and Prevention

## What it is
Cross-site scripting is the injection of attacker-controlled script into a page that other
users load. The script runs with the privileges of the victim session, which makes session
theft, credential capture through injected forms, and actions performed as the victim all
possible.

Three variants matter operationally. Reflected XSS returns the payload in the response to the
request that carried it, usually via a crafted link. Stored XSS persists the payload server
side so it executes for every subsequent viewer, which makes it far more damaging. DOM-based
XSS never involves the server in the injection at all: client-side JavaScript writes untrusted
input into the page.

## Detection
Look for script tags, javascript: URLs, onerror=, onload=, onmouseover=, document.cookie,
eval(, and their URL- and HTML-encoded equivalents appearing in request parameters, form
fields, headers such as Referer and User-Agent, and file names. Content Security Policy
violation reports are a high-signal source: they fire when a page tries to execute script from
an unexpected origin.

Stored XSS often shows first as an unusual outbound request from many user browsers to one
unfamiliar host - the exfiltration channel.

## Triage
Determine the variant. For stored XSS, find every record holding the payload and every user
who has rendered it since. Check whether session cookies carry HttpOnly; without it, assume
session tokens were captured. Review authentication logs for sessions used from unexpected
addresses after the exposure window opened.

## Containment
Remove the stored payload. Invalidate sessions for users who may have rendered it. Deploy or
tighten Content Security Policy. Where a parameter is the vector, filter it at the WAF while
the code fix is prepared.

## Prevention
Encode on output, contextually - HTML body, attribute, JavaScript and URL contexts each need
different encoding. Prefer frameworks that escape by default and avoid innerHTML,
document.write and eval. Set HttpOnly and Secure on session cookies. Deploy a strict
Content Security Policy. Validate input by allowlist, treating it as defence in depth rather
than the primary control.
